Coordinate with your team before doing this'; team members should re-clone: 'Do not use git pull - it will bring back the old history!'; contact the hosting provider for server-side cleanup if needed. The Azure Repos page 'Set Git repository permissions' (read 2026-11-18) lists 'Force push (rewrite history, delete branches and tags)', not set for any security group by default; the storage page 'Manage storage account access keys' (read 2026-11-18) gives the rotation order: point applications at the secondary key, regenerate the primary, update, then regenerate the secondary, and warns that regenerating a key affects every client using it.

brief.situation: You are the DevOps engineer at Marlow Logistics. The carrier SDK repository in Azure Repos is to be mirrored to a public GitHub repository at 16:00, announced to partners. A pre-release secret scan found a storage account key in config/local.settings.json, committed in March and deleted in a later commit. The key still works: the tracking service in production uses it.
handover: Production's tracking service reads key1 of storage account stmarlowtrack from Key Vault.
Four developers have local clones; two open pull requests target main.
howItWorks: The terminal shows each command's output; the diagram shows the repository's history, the storage account key it holds, and the public mirror due at 16:00.
Each command takes a minute or two; the clock moves only when you act or wait.
When you close, you write the record and explain your reasoning.

source.note: The public mirror is announced for 16:00, 160 minutes after the scan.

effects.log: The exposed key no longer works, production kept running on key2, and the file is gone from every commit of every branch and tag. The two pull requests are recreated from the rewritten main.

writeup.question: For the record: where the key was, what you changed in what order, and what stops it coming back.

parts.label: Where
parts.modelAnswer: The key was added in 4e1a9c0 and deleted in 9d2b113, so it sat in 37 historical versions; it matched key1, which production's tracking service used through Key Vault.

parts.label: Order
parts.modelAnswer: Tracking moved to key2, key1 was regenerated, then filter-repo removed the file from every commit and the branches and tags were force-pushed. Regenerating both keys would have cut production off; a deletion commit changes nothing.

parts.label: Prevention
parts.modelAnswer: Developers re-clone instead of pulling, the force-push grant is removed, and secret push protection blocks a key at push time.

expertPath.text: Key in 37 versions; it is key1, used by tracking via Key Vault; force push needs a grant.
Tracking to key2; regenerate key1; filter-repo; force push; re-clone notice, permission reset, push protection.

trackingDown.headline: Rotate one key at a time
trackingDown.body: Move consumers to the other key, then regenerate the exposed one. Regenerating both at once is an outage.

keyPublished.headline: Deleting the file is not removing it
keyPublished.body: A later deletion leaves every earlier commit intact. Rotate the secret, then rewrite history, before the repository goes public.

scrubbed.headline: Good: rotate, rewrite, prevent
scrubbed.body: You found every commit with the key, confirmed it was live and who used it, rotated it one key at a time, removed it from all history with filter-repo, verified, and closed the path back in.

scoring.modelReasoning: The key is still in history even though a later commit deleted the file, and it is live: production uses key1. Move tracking to key2, regenerate key1, then remove the file from every commit with git filter-repo and force-push, so the mirror publishes clean history behind a dead key. Regenerating both keys at once is an outage; a deletion commit leaves history unchanged. Then have everyone re-clone, remove the force-push grant and turn on push protection.
